1:
When Abraham married Keturah is the first question, and it divides the writers sharply. Henry and Wesley take the plain order of the narrative: he had buried Sarah and married off Isaac, the two dear companions of his life, and was now solitary, his household wanting a governess, so he took Keturah, probably the chief of his maidservants; marriage, Henry adds, is not forbidden to old age. Gill dates it three years after Sarah's death, when Abraham was a hundred and forty. Calvin calls that reading very absurd. Abraham was dead in his own body thirty-eight years before Sarah died, and when Paul commends his faith he asserts that the body of the father was dead as well as the womb of the mother; it would be unworthy of the man's gravity, and at variance with the apostle, that one who at a hundred was cold and impotent should forty years afterwards father many sons. Gill, though he dates the marriage late, reports a bishop's opinion that answers Calvin's difficulty: that Abraham took Keturah as a concubine some twenty years after marrying Sarah, when she proved barren, and long before he took Hagar, the notice being deferred so that the thread of the history should not be broken. He supports it from her being called a concubine, and from Abraham's having great-grandchildren by her before he died. Ellicott holds the matter undecided, since the Hebrew says only that Abraham added and took a wife; it is possible that Isaac's marriage left him solitary and he took Keturah then, the sole objection being his own words that it was beyond nature for a man of a hundred to have a son.

On one point Ellicott and Calvin agree against the Jewish commentators, who cut the knot by identifying Keturah with Hagar and crediting her in the meantime with a matronly devotion to the bringing up of Ishmael. Both refuse it, and both refuse it from the same verse, where the gifts made to the sons of the concubines plainly allude to two women and not one. Ellicott also weighs an argument used on the other side, that the marriage must fall in Sarah's lifetime because grandchildren are named a verse later; he thinks it carries little weight, since those names may have been added afterwards to bring the genealogy down.

Of the six sons, Ellicott says the supposed traces of their names in Arabia are untrustworthy, though Josephus and Jerome place the family in Arabia Felix. Clarke is readier to look for them, offering a city named from Zimran on the authority of Stephanus Byzantinus while thinking it likelier, with Calmet, that all these sons lived in Arabia Deserta; he reports that several learned men identify Jokshan with the father of the Arabs, gives Medan and Midian to the country east of the Dead Sea, and derives the brook Jabbok from Ishbak and the Sacceans from Shuah. Keil and Delitzsch work the second generation out the same way, connecting Sheba with the Sabaeans who stole Job's oxen and Dedan with the traders named beside Tema, and matching Dedan's three sons with tribes in Hejas and as far as Mesopotamia. Ellicott singles out the one name with a future. Midian's race became famous traders, and since the Hebrew calls the same men Medanites in one verse and Midianites in another it is probable the two tribes coalesced; Jethro belonged to them, and enriched by commerce they grew dangerous neighbours to Israel. He adds that Bildad the Shuhite may have come of Shuah. Henry looks past the names to the promise, seeing in six sons born so late a part-fulfilment of what was promised about the increase of Abraham's posterity, and Wesley puts the point after him: the strength Abraham received by the promise still remained in him, to show how far the virtue of a promise exceeds the power of nature.
3:
That Abraham gave all he had to Isaac is qualified at once by Gill, who takes it of a last will rather than a delivery in his lifetime: he plainly reserved something for himself and for gifts to the others, as his servant had told Rebekah's family, so the words may be rendered had given, or else mean that what he had purposed he now actually performed. Clarke reckons the estate as the principal flocks and, above all, the right to Canaan, with the confirmation to Isaac and his posterity of everything contained in the promises. Wesley makes it a matter of justice rather than favour, since Abraham owed it to Sarah his first wife and to Rebekah, who had married Isaac on the assurance of it.

Gill explains what a concubine was in this household, since Hagar and Keturah are both elsewhere called wives. They were concubine wives, half wives or secondary ones; the Jewish writers say they were espoused but not by writing as full wives were, stood under the lawful wife where there was one, ranked as head servants, and their children did not inherit. Clarke guesses at the gifts, cattle for breeding, seed for sowing and implements of husbandry, and explains the sending away as a precaution: Abraham did it while he lived, lest after his death they should dispute a settlement in the land of promise with Isaac. From that circumstance, he says, arose the law prevailing in almost every country by which the estate goes to the eldest son of a lawful wife; concubines were perfectly legitimate then, but their children did not inherit except on failure of legal issue and by the lawful wife's consent, and Calmet notes that it was by consent of Leah and Rachel that the children of their slaves shared equally. Clarke adds a parallel from Solon, whose law excluded all natural children from the paternal inheritance while allowing the father to make them a present not exceeding a thousand drachmas.

Calvin looks at the dismissal itself and admits how it appears. To constitute one son sole heir and send the others away with gifts was apparently harsh and cruel; but it was agreeable to the appointment of God, so that the whole possession of the land might remain to Isaac's posterity, and it was not lawful for Abraham to divide at his own pleasure an inheritance granted entire to another. Calvin is careful that no one take it for a precedent. A man who now singled out one son as heir and disinherited the rest would do them injury, and by applying the torch of injustice would light a flame of pernicious strife in his family; the special reason must be noted by which Abraham was not merely induced but compelled, namely that the grant made to Isaac should not be disturbed. On where the others went, Clarke names Arabia Deserta, east of Beersheba, and Ellicott extends it to Arabia and southern Mesopotamia, where by their superior vigour and organisation the descendants of Abraham established their supremacy over the natives. Ellicott closes with an observation from Burckhardt, that the Bedaween still follow Abraham's practice: when the children are grown each younger son is given his share, whereupon he moves off and leaves the eldest brother in quiet possession of the home. Keil and Delitzsch, whose note begins here, take up the phrase that will describe Abraham's own end. To be gathered to his people is constantly distinguished from dying and from being buried, and means reunion in Sheol with friends already gone; the expression therefore presupposes a belief in the personal continuance of a man after death, which in the patriarchs the promises of God had raised from a presentiment into a firm assurance of faith.
7:
Clarke thinks the phrase the days of the years has a beauty too little regarded. Good men do not live by centuries, nor even count their lives by years, but by days, as though they were the creatures only of a day, having no more time than they can call their own and spending that day with reference to eternity. Calvin counts the same span as a pilgrimage: Abraham deserves praise for wonderful and incomparable patience, having wandered a hundred years while God led him about, content in life and death with the bare promise. Let those be ashamed, he says, who find it hard to bear the disquiet of a year or two, since the father of the faithful was not merely a stranger for a century but often cast into exile besides; what sustained him was the knowledge that his life was the object of divine care. Ellicott works the arithmetic out to a domestic result. Abraham was seventy-five when he left Haran, so his sojourn in Canaan lasted a hundred years, a quarter of it spent in the trial of his faith before Isaac was given; and since the twins were born when Isaac was sixty, they were fifteen when their grandfather died and had probably often seen him. Wesley sums it in a line: he was a sojourner in a strange country a hundred years.

On the words gave up the ghost, Clarke dissents from a version he otherwise values highly. The Hebrew verb signifies to pant for breath, to cease breathing, to expire, and everywhere the simple word expired would be the proper rendering; for since ghost now means only the immortal spirit, and giving up a spirit is no act proper to man, the familiar phrase says more than the original does. Calvin quarrels with a different inference. Those are mistaken, he holds, who take the words for a sudden death, as though Abraham had not been worn out by long disease but expired without pain; Moses means that the father of the faithful was not exempt from the common lot, so our minds should not languish when the outward man perishes but suffer this frail tabernacle to be dissolved with tranquillity, in view of the renovation laid up for our hope. No feebleness of body, failing of the eyes or trembling of the hands should so dishearten us that we do not hasten after our father's example with joy to our death. Gill takes the reading Calvin rejects, and has Abraham give up the ghost readily and cheerfully, with no previous sickness and no pain, going out by mere decay of nature.

Wesley finds in the good old age both a discharge and a crown, adding that a good man dies full of days even if he does not die old, satisfied with living here and longing for a better place; and on being gathered to his people he distinguishes the two gatherings, the body to the congregation of the dead and the soul to the congregation of the blessed, death gathering each of us to our own. Keil and Delitzsch notice who buried him: Isaac and Ishmael together, since Ishmael, though shut out from the covenant, had been acknowledged by God as Abraham's son in a distinct blessing, and so stood above Keturah's sons. They add that the blessing passed to Isaac, who settled by Hagar's well, having been there already. Henry marks the same transfer as the point of the verse, that the blessing of Abraham did not die with him but survived to all the children of the promise; Clarke is less sanguine about the heir, asking how little we hear in Isaac of the work of faith, the patience of hope and the labour of love, and observing that only one Abraham ever appeared where there should have been many imitators.
12:
All four agree that Ishmael's genealogy is here to show a promise kept. Gill puts it shortly, that the Lord was not unmindful of what he had said about multiplying Abraham's seed. Clarke sees the writer showing how the promises were fulfilled to both branches, Isaac's blessing having just been noticed and Ishmael's increase now proved. Keil and Delitzsch note that by the settled plan of Genesis this account precedes the history of Isaac, and that the twelve sons are given as princes of the tribes which sprang from them. Ellicott states the rule the book follows: Ishmael is not dismissed without a short record, after which he falls into the background and the historian returns to his main subject, the preparation of that race of whom Christ came. He adds a reason for keeping such notices at all, that it was God's purpose the Jewish Messiah should be the Redeemer of the Gentiles too, so that from the first these histories were not alien to his counsels. Calvin values the fulfilment as evidence of God's veracity, and thinks it no common gift that Ishmael should have twelve sons holding rank over as many tribes; but he is careful to call the benefit adventitious, since it was superadded to the spiritual covenant, and he observes that once the towns are enumerated Moses buries the whole race in oblivion, so that a substantial perpetuity remains only in the Church.

The names are traced with the usual caution and the usual disagreement. Keil connects Nebajoth and Kedar with the rich flock-owners of Isaiah and, on the current opinion which Wetzstein disputes, with Pliny's Nabataeans; these held Arabia Petraea with Petra for their capital and spread south and north-east, so that their name was afterwards given to all the tribes east of Jordan and became a common term for Chaldeans and Syrians alike. Ellicott follows several of the twelve into later Scripture instead: Nebajoth and Kedar as pastoral tribes rich in flocks, Dumah as the subject of a prophecy of its own, Tema as generous and hospitable and elsewhere as active traders, and Jetur and Naphish among the Hagarite tribes conquered by Reuben, Jetur giving his name to the Iturea of the Gospel.

On the towns and castles the two differ more sharply. Clarke takes the first for places of encampment in the wilderness, such as the Arabs have used from the remotest times, and the second for towers, probably mountain tops, fortified rocks and fastnesses in wooded or hilly country. Ellicott denies there were any towns or castles in the wilderness of Paran and defines both words from their use elsewhere. The first means an unwalled village, described exactly in Leviticus, and though unwalled it was a settled and permanent dwelling; the second, rendered castle here but standing for tent in the Psalms, is really a cluster of tents, the movable encampment of a tribe. Wesley marks the close of the line rather than its spread, taking Ishmael's hundred and thirty-seven years as recorded to show the efficacy of Abraham's prayer, O that Ishmael might live before thee; he too was gathered to his people, and he died in the presence of all his brethren, with his friends about him, which Wesley thinks a thing anyone might wish for. From the distinction between the two words Ellicott draws an ethnography. The Arabs fall into two classes, the tent-dwellers who are always shifting from station to station within limits they seldom pass, and the agricultural sort with fixed habitations, who are reckoned inferiors, are probably the remains of a conquered race, and to this day pay a kind of rent or blackmail to the nobler Arabs. The distinction already existed, he says, when this tôldôth was drawn up, the farming Arabs living in their unwalled villages while the nomads pitched, now here and now there, their clusters of black camels'-hair tents.
19:
With Ishmael dismissed the narrative returns to its main line, and Gill and Calvin mark the turn: what was said of the Ishmaelites was incidental, and Moses takes up the subject he is really concerned with, which Calvin calls the progress of the Church. Clarke notes that a new section of the law begins. Calvin observes that Rebekah is expressly called the sister of Laban the Syrian, afterwards Jacob's father-in-law, of whom there would be much to relate. Henry finds the arrangement odd. The entrance of these twins into the world is, unusually, the most considerable part of their story, and little is told of Isaac himself except what bears on his father while he lived and on his sons afterwards; Isaac, he thinks, was no man of action nor much tried, but spent his days in quietness and silence.

How long the barrenness lasted is reckoned slightly differently. Henry has Isaac married at forty and a father at sixty, so twenty years childless; Clarke makes it nineteen from the same figures. Both draw the same lesson, Henry putting it that though the accomplishment of God's promise is always sure it is often slow, and seems crossed by Providence, so that the faith of believers may be tried and mercies long waited for be the more welcome. He notices too what Isaac did not do while the mercy was delayed: he did not approach a handmaid's bed, as Abraham had done and Jacob would, for he loved Rebekah. Calvin presses hardest. Nothing, he says, seems less accordant with reason than that the propagation of the Church should be so small and so slow. Abraham in extreme old age received what looks like a slender solace for his long privation, all his hope centred in one man; Isaac, himself bordering on old age, was still not a father. Where then was the seed that should equal the stars for number, and who would not suppose God was dealing deceitfully in leaving those houses empty? His answer is that the twenty years were meant so, that despair might give the greater lustre to a blessing suddenly granted.

On the prayer Gill notes that the word implies earnest and constant supplication, and reports the alternative rendering before his wife, she being present and joining in it. Clarke thinks the form of the original worth notice, since Isaac entreated the Lord directly and purposely for his wife; he cites Ainsworth for their praying together, and the rabbins for the tradition that the two went to Mount Moriah, where Isaac had once been bound, and prayed there for a son. Clarke sees a pattern too, God exercising Isaac's faith before Jacob's birth as he had Abraham's before Isaac's. Calvin prefers the simpler rendering to the one that brings Rebekah into the clause, and takes the recourse to prayer as evidence of two things Isaac knew: that he was childless because God had not blessed him, and that fruitfulness is a special gift. Though the favour of offspring was spread over the whole race when God said increase and multiply, he distributes the power in various degrees, to show men are not born fortuitously; so Isaac acknowledges that what is not at man's disposal must be sought of God. Calvin adds that this was no new thought after twenty years of disappointment: Moses says in a single word that he obtained offspring by prayer, but reason dictates that the praying had gone on for years. Wesley states the principle, that God's promises must not supersede our prayers but encourage them, and that Isaac, having prayed many years unheard, did not leave off. Keil and Delitzsch give the reason for the delay: the seed of the promise had to be prayed for from the Lord, so that it might not be taken merely for a fruit of nature but received and recognised as a gift of grace.
22:
The struggle in the womb is read by all as a sign, but they differ on what Rebekah's cry amounts to. Gill calls the motion extraordinary, the two striving as if for mastery, and takes it for an emblem of the difference between Esau and Jacob, of the contentions of their offspring, and of the conflict between flesh and spirit in good men themselves. Clarke translates the verb as dashing against or bruising each other, so violent that the mother feared for her own safety and her children's, and reads her broken words as meaning, if I must suffer such things, why did I ever wish for a child — a speech not uncommon, he says, in a first pregnancy. Keil and Delitzsch hear something graver, an evil omen that the pregnancy so long entreated would end in misfortune and the fruit of her womb miss the promised blessing, so that she cries in intense excitement, wherefore am I alive? Calvin rejects Clarke's reading outright. Those are mistaken, he says, who attribute the complaint to female impatience, since it was extorted not by pain but by abhorrence of a prodigy: she saw that such a conflict had no natural cause but portended a dreadful end, and felt the fear of divine anger stealing over her, as the faithful trace an evil to its source and tremble at the apprehension of judgment. He grants she was at first more disturbed than she should have been, but she soon found a remedy, and by her example we learn not to indulge sorrow excessively in perplexing affairs.

How she enquired of the Lord nobody knows, and three say so. Keil reports the guesses — prayer and sacrifice at a place dedicated to Jehovah, or application to a prophet, whether Abraham, Melchizedek or, on Luther's suggestion, Shem — and observes that consulting a prophet was frequent in later Israel but improbable in the patriarchal age. Clarke canvasses the same names and rules out Shem, supposed to have died ten years before, while allowing that Abraham was still alive; he adds the wry remark that she went to enquire of the Lord as women now consult a physician, intercourse with God being less common than in those times of primitive simplicity. Wesley mentions Melchizedek as the possible oracle, or some Urim or Teraphim, and turns the uncertainty to use: the word and prayer by which we now enquire give great relief to the perplexed, it being a mighty ease to spread our case before the Lord. Ellicott refuses the conjectures. God spoke directly, as of old to Adam and Eve; we read of no appearance and must not invent one, since the manner has not been revealed and it is enough to know that Jehovah did speak to men.

The answer comes as poetry, four lines on Ellicott's arrangement, and he takes them in order: the second shows that even in childhood the sons would be unlike in character and unfriendly; then follows their growth into hostile nations, and last the prediction that the son who began with the birthright, the stronger body and the greater force of arms would nevertheless end in the inferior place. Ellicott names a secondary cause, Jacob's people being settled by Joseph in the fruitful Delta and constantly reinforced by Semitic immigrants. Clarke quotes Bishop Newton for the principle governing the whole oracle, that these prophecies were meant not so much of single persons as of whole nations, since what was predicted of the brothers was verified not in themselves but in their posterity; who but the Author of life, Newton asks, could foresee that two children in one womb would multiply into two nations so unlike in manners, customs and religion as to be at perpetual variance? Keil, whose note runs into the birth, derives the boys' names from its circumstances, Esau the hairy one and Jacob the heel-holder.
24:
Both boys are named from their birth. Of the first, Gill records that the red was either his body or the hair covering it, and passes on Jarchi's reading that it foretold a shedder of blood, as he and his posterity proved. Clarke takes it for red hair all over, confirmed later when Rebekah had to use kid-skins on Jacob's hands and neck; on the name he is uncertain, since the root may mean made or perfected while the Arabic gives to make firm, and he guesses the child was so called for seeming more robust than his brother. Ellicott makes the redness a secondary reason for the later name Edom, notes that the words describing the down are elsewhere used of the sheepskin jacket worn by prophets, and takes the covering for a sign of a vigorous but sensual nature; he reports the Jewish derivation, well-made, while preferring the usual sense, hairy. Wesley says he was red and hairy as though already grown, an indication of a strong constitution, while Jacob was smooth and tender as other children.

On the second name Clarke and Ellicott part. Clarke derives it from a verb meaning to defraud, that is, to overthrow a man by tripping his heels, and takes the grasp as emblematic of Jacob's supplanting his brother; Wesley reads it the same way, as signifying both the pursuit of the birthright from the first and the eventual prevailing for it. Ellicott denies that the phrase describes a grasp at all. Twins are usually born an hour or more apart, and the words mean only that here there was no interval, which he calls a rare but recorded occurrence; the name signifies one who follows at another's heels, and it was Esau who first put a bad sense on it, riveted there afterwards by Jacob's own conduct. He adds that those who defend the literal reading from Hosea know only the English, since the Hebrew there says he heeled his brother, that is, overreached him; and he objects that supplant is a poor rendering, containing a different metaphor.

The grown men are drawn by contrast. Keil and Delitzsch have Esau wandering the fields and Jacob one whose disposition found pleasure in the quiet of home, sitting in the tents rather than merely dwelling in them. Ellicott presses the word used of Jacob, rendered plain here and perfect elsewhere, and holds both wrong: it conveys no idea of blamelessness but only of general integrity, and should everywhere be translated upright. Calvin reads the same word antithetically rather than as praise, Moses setting the mild disposition of a man who loved home so much that he might seem indolent against the vigour of a brother addicted to hunting. Wesley allows both senses, an honest man who dealt fairly, and one who kept to the tents either as shepherd or as a student frequenting the tents of Melchizedek. Henry has Esau hunt with such dexterity that he became a conqueror ruling his neighbours, while Jacob liked the true delights of retirement better than all pretended pleasures, a stranger and pilgrim in spirit and a shepherd all his days. On the divided affections Gill and Ellicott explain Isaac's taste literally, the venison being in his mouth, that is, to his liking, and Ellicott adds that a man wanting physical vigour, as the children of aged parents commonly are, both admired the energy Esau had from his mother and relished its fruits. Henry warns that godly parents may feel their affections drawn to a godly child yet must not show partiality, lest evils arise. Calvin turns the partiality into evidence: God let Esau be so preferred in his father's affection that Jacob looked a rejected man, precisely to show that his election needs no assistance and can overcome any obstacle, so that it is intolerable presumption to make that adoption depend on the will of man.
29:
Gill notes that boiling broth was no usual employment of Jacob's, and passes on the Targum's tradition that this was the day Abraham died, lentils being the food of mourners; from which the Jewish writers reckon the twins to have been fifteen. On the dish Gill adds that lentils were much used in Egypt, that Alexandria was famous for them, and that those of Pelusium are named by Virgil and Martial. Clarke supplies a traveller's description from Barbary, where lentils dissolve easily into a mass and make a pottage of a chocolate colour, which he identifies with the red pottage of the story. Calvin attends to how Esau asks for it. The Hebrew runs, feed me with that red, that red, the word pottage being left out; the repetition of the epithet and the omission of the noun show the haste and eagerness of the man, whose eye was caught by the colour while hunger left him careless of consequences.

Whether Esau's plea was true is treated seriously. Clarke thinks the transaction shows he was so exhausted that he must have perished without immediate refreshment, having returned from the field too spent to make his own preparations. Calvin allows that in desiring and asking food he does nothing worthy of reprehension, and grants that a man who names a dish by its colour only is plainly indifferent to delicacies; but the next words undo him. When he says, behold, I am at the point to die, and what profit shall this birthright do to me, he betrays a profane desire wholly addicted to the earth and the flesh. Wesley reaches the same verdict by another road, granting that if the birthright were only a temporal advantage there was something true in what Esau said, since worldly enjoyments stand us in no stead in a dying hour; but the thing being spiritual, his undervaluing of it was the greatest profaneness imaginable, and it is egregious folly to part with our interest in God and heaven for the riches of this world.

What was actually sold is disputed. Gill lists honour and authority next to the parents, a double portion, the parental blessing, and above all the promises of the Messiah and the inheritance of Canaan as a type of the heavenly one, mentioning the priesthood as claimed by some but questioned; he supposes Rebekah knew from the oracle that these were designed for Jacob and had advised him accordingly. Clarke gives the same list as the general supposition, then reports Calmet controverting most of it with apparent reason, holding the double portion the only incontestable right of the first-born, the rest conceded rather than fixed by law. Henry calls the birthright Esau's by providence but Jacob's by promise, a spiritual privilege carrying the excellency of dignity and of power as well as the double portion. On the buyer he is exactly balanced: Jacob is to be commended for coveting earnestly the best gifts, having grown acquainted with spiritual blessings in his tents while Esau lost the scent of them in the field, but he cannot be justified in taking advantage of a brother's necessity, nor was such an indirect course agreeable to his character as a plain man. Wesley says the same of both parties in a line. Calvin is harshest on the scene, calling it little different from the sport of children and asking what kind of bargain this was, since Jacob ought of his own accord to have satisfied his brother's hunger and, refusing, is open to the charge of inhumanity. His answer is that God was proving Esau's disposition in a small matter and bringing to light what lay hid in both; and he warns against suspending Jacob's election on a foreseen worthiness, since Paul, having declared election gratuitous, denies that the distinction is to be looked for in the persons.
32:
Gill canvasses what Esau meant by saying he was at the point to die. He may have spoken of the common frailty of life, or, as Aben Ezra suggests, of the danger he ran among wild beasts; but Gill thinks he meant his present faintness, which unless relieved must end in death, and mentions Lightfoot's opinion that this fell in the famine of the next chapter. On the oath Gill sees a precaution, binding Esau to let his brother enjoy the birthright undisputed. Calvin defends the demand: Jacob acted with no cruelty, since he took nothing from Esau but only sought confirmation of a right divinely granted him already, and did so with a pious intention, to establish the certainty of his own election. What Calvin will not excuse is the seller. Esau's infatuation is that in the name and presence of God he does not hesitate to put his birthright to sale; he had rushed on the food under the impulse of hunger, but when an oath came to be exacted some sense of religion should have stolen over him to correct his brutal cupidity, and instead he makes God himself a witness of his ingratitude.

Gill observes that Jacob gave more than was bargained for, bread as well as pottage, though nothing until the oath was taken; and he sums the pair up by saying that, cunning as Esau was and plain as Jacob was, the plain man outwitted the cunning one. On the four short verbs that follow, Calvin asks why so flat a sentence should be recorded and answers that it carries great weight. It commends the piety of Jacob, who was no log of wood and, in preparing food, must have sharpened his own hunger, so that he had to do violence to himself to bear it, and could never have subdued his flesh unless a spiritual desire of a better life flourished within him. On the other side the four words describe Esau's indifference exactly, and are there so that we may understand what follows, that he reckoned the incomparable benefit he had lost as nothing. Ellicott reads the same clause as graphic: there is no regret in it, no sad feeling that he had prolonged his life at too high a cost.

Whether the buyer is better than the seller divides them. Clarke will not have it. The apostle calls Esau profane, and rightly, since he should have perished rather than alienate such a right; but what, Clarke asks, of his most unnatural brother, who refused a starving man a morsel unless he gave up his birthright? Surely, he concludes, he who bought it in such circumstances was as bad as he who sold it, and by this act Jacob verified his claim to the name of supplanter. Ellicott grants the meanness and still finds a difference, since Jacob at least valued the privileges; and he traces the sequel as reward and punishment together. Jacob was confirmed in the birthright and became progenitor of the chosen race, yet from this day his life was full of danger and difficulty, fleeing his brother's enmity and falling perpetually victim to fraud and cruel deceit. Gradually, Ellicott says, his character ripened, until the scheming Jacob became an Israel, and in his pious old age we see a man full of trust and faith, unworldly and unselfish, purified of his early infirmities and strengthened by sorrow. Gill's last word is on the other brother, who went off about his former course with no remorse and no repentance, and sought the blessing with tears only when his father lay dying. Wesley agrees and adds the aggravation: Esau used no means to get the bargain revoked and made no appeal to his father about it, so that what necessity might have excused his profaneness confirmed, and by his later neglect and contempt he put it past recall.
